common.sentence: This river has a bridge; without it, only a boat could get us across.

common.sentence: My schedule is full; I wish I had more free time.

common.sentence: I don't know the answer; I wish I knew it.

common.sentence: The rent takes half my pay; I wish it cost less.

common.sentence: Our office bans pets; I wish I could bring my dog.

common.sentence: My friends live far away; I wish they lived nearby.

common.sentence: I speak too quickly in meetings; I wish I spoke more slowly.

common.sentence: I have a headache; I wish I didn't feel so bad.

common.sentence: I owe money on my car; I wish I had no debt.

common.sentence: The winning design was chosen by the visitors, not the staff.

common.sentence: The project instructions say each sample must be numbered separately.

common.sentence: Should the loose handle be tightened before we use the cart?

common.sentence: The repair shop says my lamp will be ready tomorrow; its cord will be replaced.

common.sentence: At this workshop, the lids are made of recycled plastic.

common.sentence: In this kit, the brush is used to apply the glue.

common.sentence: The repair estimate includes labor, but the final charge may differ.

common.sentence: For this order, the shelf will be cut to fit the alcove.

common.sentence: The service desk expects the screen repair to be completed tomorrow.
common.meaning: to be finished by someone

language_specific.usage: Expect something to be completed expresses a prediction that someone will finish it; it does not promise the result.

common.sentence: Maya said that the side door was unlocked.
common.meaning: expressed something in words

language_specific.usage: Say can introduce a content clause: say that something is true. Said is the past form of say.

common.sentence: I said to Marcus that his package had arrived.
common.meaning: spoke words to someone

language_specific.usage: Say something to someone, or say to someone that something is true. Said is the past form of say.

common.sentence: Nina told us that the meeting would start late.
common.meaning: informed someone in words

language_specific.usage: Tell someone that something is true; the recipient comes before the content clause. Told is the past form of tell.

common.sentence: The caller told me her name before hanging up.
common.meaning: gave someone information

language_specific.usage: Tell someone something; a noun phrase can follow the recipient. Told is the past form of tell.

common.sentence: Please tell me about your first day at work.
common.meaning: give someone an account

language_specific.usage: Tell someone about something; the recipient comes before the about phrase.

common.sentence: The note says to leave the keys inside.
common.meaning: contains the written message

language_specific.usage: A written message can say to do something. Says is the third-person singular present form of say.

common.sentence: The label says that this sauce contains peanuts.
common.meaning: states something in writing

language_specific.usage: A label can say that something is true. Says is the third-person singular present form of say.

common.sentence: When I thanked her, Rosa said, “You're welcome.”
common.meaning: spoke the quoted words

language_specific.usage: Say can introduce a person's exact words in a quotation. Said is the past form of say.

common.sentence: Please say hello to your parents for me.
common.meaning: give someone a greeting

language_specific.usage: Say hello to someone; for me identifies the person whose greeting is being passed on.

common.sentence: Could you tell Luis hello when you see him?
common.meaning: pass a greeting to someone

language_specific.usage: Tell someone hello is an informal way to ask another person to pass on a greeting.

common.sentence: He didn't say anything about a change in plans.
common.meaning: mention any information

language_specific.usage: In a negative clause, say anything about something means mention any information about it. Use the base form say after didn't.

common.sentence: Did the guide tell you where the trail begins?
common.meaning: give someone information

language_specific.usage: Tell someone where something is or happens; the where clause has statement word order. Use tell after did.

common.sentence: Please tell the truth about what happened to the vase.
common.meaning: say what really happened

language_specific.usage: In this sense, truth is noncount and has no plural; use the in the fixed phrase tell the truth. A recipient is optional; about introduces the subject.

common.sentence: Grandpa told a story about his first summer job.
common.meaning: gave an account of events

language_specific.usage: Tell a story can be used without a stated listener. Story is countable: one story, two stories. Told is the past form of tell.

common.sentence: The coach had something to say about our teamwork.
common.meaning: a comment to make

language_specific.usage: Have something to say about a subject means have a comment to make about it.

common.sentence: Is the library closed today? The website doesn't say so.
common.meaning: state that the library is closed today

language_specific.usage: Say so refers back to a stated or understood claim. So follows say; it does not name a recipient.

common.sentence: She said goodbye to the guests at the door.
common.meaning: give someone a farewell

language_specific.usage: Say goodbye to someone. Said is the past form of say.

common.sentence: The message didn't say who had called earlier.
common.meaning: give the information

language_specific.usage: Say can introduce a clause identifying a person. Use the base form say after didn't.

common.sentence: I broke the cup, but I might tell a lie and blame the cat.
common.meaning: deliberately say something false

language_specific.usage: Lie is a count noun: tell a lie or tell lies. You can tell someone a lie; the recipient comes before a lie.

common.sentence: You visited Alaska? Tell me more about your trip.
common.meaning: please give me further information

language_specific.usage: Tell someone more about something; the object pronoun me follows tell, and about introduces the subject.
language_specific.social: Here the request shows interest in the other person's trip.

common.sentence: Yesterday, Leah said she was tired after her flight.
common.meaning: describes Leah's state when she spoke

language_specific.usage: Was agrees with she. In a report after said, was can describe a state at the time of speaking; a present form may be backshifted.

common.sentence: At lunch, Ben said he needed a ride home.
common.meaning: required something

language_specific.usage: After a past reporting verb, needed can report a need Ben described at the time; the report does not establish whether he still needs a ride.

common.sentence: On Monday, I said I was working from home.
common.meaning: was doing my job

language_specific.usage: Was working describes work in progress at the time of the reported statement. Was agrees with I.

common.sentence: Yesterday, Carla said she had lost her wallet before lunch.
common.meaning: had become unable to find something

language_specific.usage: Had lost places the loss before Carla's reported statement. Lost is the past participle of lose.

common.sentence: By Friday, Omar said he had finished the report.
common.meaning: had completed something

language_specific.usage: Had finished places completion before Omar's reported statement. A present perfect in the original statement can be reported this way after said.

common.sentence: At breakfast, Dad said he would call the dentist.
common.meaning: would contact someone by phone

language_specific.usage: Would call can report a future intention described in a past statement; it does not establish whether the call happened.

common.sentence: Last week, Priya said she could drive us there.
common.meaning: was able to take someone by car

language_specific.usage: Could drive can report an ability stated with can after a past reporting verb. The report does not establish whether Priya drove.

common.sentence: On Tuesday, Sam said the store was closing at six.
common.meaning: was scheduled to stop serving customers

language_specific.usage: Was closing can report a closing time described as planned at the time of Sam's statement. Was agrees with the singular subject store.

common.sentence: At noon, Eva said she had already eaten breakfast.
common.meaning: had finished eating before the statement
common.part_of_speech: past perfect verb phrase with adverb

language_specific.usage: Had eaten places the meal before Eva's statement. Eaten is the past participle of eat; already can appear between had and eaten.

common.sentence: Yesterday, Leo said his sister lived near the station.
common.meaning: had a home somewhere

language_specific.usage: Lived can report where someone lived at the time of a past statement. It does not say whether she still lives there.

common.sentence: Mia said, “I'll call tomorrow.” That evening, I reported that Mia would call the next day.
common.meaning: the day after the statement

language_specific.usage: The next day relates the time to Mia's statement; tomorrow in her words refers to that same day.

common.sentence: At the station, Ana said, “I'm here.” Later at home, I reported that Ana was there.
common.meaning: at the station

language_specific.usage: There refers to Ana's location at the station; here in her words refers to that same location.

common.sentence: Yesterday, the teacher explained that water freezes at 32 degrees Fahrenheit.
common.meaning: turns from liquid into ice

language_specific.usage: The present freezes agrees with water and can remain present after a past reporting verb when the statement expresses a continuing fact.

common.sentence: Yesterday, Nora said her brother is a nurse; he still works at the hospital.
common.meaning: identifies someone's occupation

language_specific.usage: Is agrees with the singular subject brother. A present form can be retained after said when the information remains relevant.

common.sentence: At dinner, I said I had seen the film before.
common.meaning: had watched something

language_specific.usage: Had seen places the viewing before the reported statement. Seen is the past participle of see.

common.sentence: Yesterday, Kim said the guests had left before the rain started.
common.meaning: had gone away

language_specific.usage: Had left places the departure before both the rain and Kim's statement. Left is the past participle of leave.

common.sentence: At noon, Julia said she didn't know the result yet.
common.meaning: did not have the information

language_specific.usage: Didn't know reports a lack of knowledge at the time of Julia's statement. Use the base form know after didn't.

common.sentence: Last night, Eric said the package would arrive this morning.
common.meaning: was expected to reach its destination

language_specific.usage: Would arrive reports an expected event future to Eric's statement. The report does not establish whether it arrived.

common.sentence: After class, Hana said she had already sent the email.
common.meaning: had caused something to go to a recipient before the statement
common.part_of_speech: past perfect verb phrase with adverb

language_specific.usage: Had sent places the sending before Hana's statement. Sent is the past participle of send; already can appear between had and sent.

common.sentence: On Friday, the manager said the office was open that afternoon.
common.meaning: was available for business

language_specific.usage: Was agrees with the singular subject office. Was open reports the office's stated availability on Friday afternoon.

common.sentence: Maya asked where the meeting was, so I gave her the address.
common.meaning: at what place

language_specific.usage: In the reported question, where introduces the place being asked about; the subject the meeting comes before was.

common.sentence: The caller asked when our store closes on Sundays.
common.meaning: at what time

language_specific.usage: In the reported question, when introduces the time being asked about; our store comes before closes. Present closes can report a current schedule.

common.sentence: I asked Leo why he had left the party early.
common.meaning: for what reason

language_specific.usage: In the reported question, why introduces the reason being asked about; he comes before had left. Had left places the departure before the question.

common.sentence: Nina wanted to know how I fixed the printer.
common.meaning: in what way

language_specific.usage: In the reported question, how introduces the method being asked about; I comes before fixed.

common.sentence: The receptionist asked if I had an appointment that afternoon.
common.meaning: introduces a reported yes-or-no question

language_specific.usage: After asked, if or whether can introduce this reported question; the subject I comes before had.

common.sentence: Dad asked whether the package had arrived before noon.
common.meaning: introduces a reported yes-or-no question

language_specific.usage: After asked, whether or if can introduce this reported question; the package comes before had arrived. Had arrived places the arrival before Dad's question.

common.sentence: The coach asked who wanted a ride home after practice.
common.meaning: what person or people

language_specific.usage: Who is the subject of wanted in this reported question, so no additional subject or did is needed.

common.sentence: I asked who the manager had chosen for the project.
common.meaning: what person or people

language_specific.usage: Who is the object of chosen; the subject the manager comes before had chosen in the reported question.

common.sentence: The technician asked what was causing the strange noise.
common.meaning: asks for the identity of a thing

language_specific.usage: What is the subject of was causing in this reported question, so it comes directly before the verb.

common.sentence: At dinner, Sam asked what we were cooking for dessert.
common.meaning: were preparing food at that time

language_specific.usage: The past progressive uses were with we, you, or a plural subject and was with I or a third-person singular subject. In the reported question, we comes before were cooking; what is its object.

common.sentence: The customer asked which jacket was available in blue.
common.meaning: what particular one or ones

language_specific.usage: Which modifies jacket. The full phrase which jacket is the subject and comes before was in the reported question.

common.sentence: I asked which route the driver recommended for the trip.
common.meaning: what particular way to travel

language_specific.usage: Route is a count noun: one route, several routes; choose a route. Which route is the object of recommended; the driver is the subject.

common.sentence: The host asked how many guests we expected for dinner.
common.meaning: what number of

language_specific.usage: How many modifies a plural count noun, here guests. In the reported question, we comes before expected.

common.sentence: My neighbor asked how long the repairs would take.
common.meaning: would require a period of time

language_specific.usage: Would is followed by the base verb take. It can report a question about a future duration from a past viewpoint; the subject the repairs comes before would.

common.sentence: A visitor asked how much the museum tickets cost.
common.meaning: what amount of money

language_specific.usage: How much asks about price here. In the reported question, the subject the museum tickets comes before cost; no do is needed.

common.sentence: I asked the librarian where I could return the book.
common.meaning: was able or permitted to give back

language_specific.usage: Could is followed by the base verb return; it can report can from a past viewpoint. In the reported question, the subject I comes before could.

common.sentence: At lunch, Omar asked if we were joining him that evening.
common.meaning: were planning to spend time with someone

language_specific.usage: The past progressive uses were with we, you, or a plural subject and was with I or a third-person singular subject. Here the question concerns a possible arrangement for later that evening; we comes before were joining.

common.sentence: The nurse asked whose phone was ringing in the waiting room.
common.meaning: belonging to what person

language_specific.usage: Whose asks about possession and modifies phone. The full phrase whose phone is the subject of was ringing.

common.sentence: The guide asked where we had come from that morning.
common.meaning: indicating the starting place of a journey

language_specific.usage: Come from connects a person or journey with an origin. In this reported question, where refers to that origin and from follows come; had come places the journey before the question.

common.sentence: I asked the clerk whether I needed to sign anything.
common.meaning: had to do something

language_specific.usage: Use need to + base verb to express necessity; needed is the past form. In the reported question, I comes before needed to sign.

common.sentence: Yesterday, Ana asked me to water her plants during her trip.
common.meaning: requested that I do something

language_specific.usage: Use ask + person + to + base verb to report a request; the person named is expected to act.

common.sentence: The instructor told us to keep our helmets on during practice.
common.meaning: instructed us to do something

language_specific.usage: Use tell + person + to + base verb to report an instruction. Told is the irregular past form of tell.

common.sentence: Ben asked me not to share his draft before Friday.
common.meaning: not to let others see or have something, as part of a reported request

language_specific.usage: For a negative reported request, use ask + recipient + not to + base verb.

common.sentence: The mechanic told me not to drive the car with that flat tire.
common.meaning: instructed me not to do something

language_specific.usage: Use tell + recipient + not to + base verb for a negative instruction. Told is the irregular past of tell.

common.sentence: The pharmacist advised me to take the medicine with food.
common.meaning: recommended that I do something

language_specific.usage: Use advise + person + to + base verb to report advice.

common.sentence: I had promised to call; Maya reminded me to do it.
common.meaning: helped me remember to do something

language_specific.usage: Use remind + person + to + base verb to report a reminder about an action.

common.sentence: The guide warned us not to touch the hot metal railing.
common.meaning: cautioned us against doing something

language_specific.usage: Use warn + person + not to + base verb to report a caution against an action.

common.sentence: The coach encouraged Lena to try again after her first attempt.
common.meaning: gave support or confidence

language_specific.usage: Use encourage + person + to + base verb to report encouragement to act.

common.sentence: The teacher instructed the class to work in pairs.
common.meaning: gave directions

language_specific.usage: Use instruct + person or group + to + base verb to report directions.

common.sentence: The stranded traveler begged a driver to stop and help.
common.meaning: asked someone urgently

language_specific.usage: Use beg + person + to + base verb to report an urgent plea.

common.sentence: Rosa told Ben, “Bring my coat.” She asked him to bring her coat.
common.meaning: belonging to Rosa

language_specific.usage: In the report, her refers to Rosa, whose own words were my coat.

common.sentence: The clouds were dark, so I urged Ben to bring a raincoat.
common.meaning: strongly advised

language_specific.usage: Use urge + person + to + base verb to report strong advice.

common.sentence: I told Kim, 'Please send the photos to my address.' I asked Kim to send me the photos.
common.meaning: the speaker, as the recipient of the photos

language_specific.usage: The original speaker uses my in the request. In the report, the same speaker uses me for the recipient. Send someone something places the recipient before the thing sent.

common.sentence: Jules said, “Call me at the hotel.” Jules asked me to call them there.
common.meaning: Jules, the person to call

language_specific.usage: Them can refer to one person. In the report it refers to Jules, who used me in the request.

common.sentence: Dad said, “Bring my glasses to work.” He asked me to bring his glasses.
common.meaning: belonging to Dad

language_specific.usage: In the report, his refers to Dad, who used my in the request.

common.sentence: On May 1, Lee asked me to submit the form the following week.
common.meaning: the week after the week of May 1

language_specific.usage: Week is a count noun: one week, two weeks; the following week identifies the week after the one containing the request.

common.sentence: Now at home, I remembered Priya asking me to leave the key at the office. I left it there.
common.meaning: at the office

language_specific.usage: There refers to the office, a place away from the reporter's current location at home.

common.sentence: The host told my sister and me, “Please take some food.” We were told to help ourselves.
common.meaning: the speaker and the speaker's sister

language_specific.usage: Ourselves refers back to we, the speaker and sister. Help oneself means to take what is offered without waiting to be served.

common.sentence: The organizer handed me a form and asked me to fill it out before the meeting.
common.meaning: complete the form

language_specific.usage: Fill out is separable: fill out the form or fill the form out. A pronoun object goes between fill and out: fill it out.

common.sentence: Nia asked, “Would you mind waiting?” She asked me to wait.
common.meaning: to stay until later

language_specific.usage: A polite request with would you mind can be reported with ask + person + to + base verb.

common.sentence: Who left this note on the kitchen table?
common.meaning: asks which person left the note

language_specific.usage: Who is the subject of left; no auxiliary is needed in this affirmative question.

common.sentence: Who did you ask about the missing package?
common.meaning: marks the past-tense question about the person you asked

language_specific.usage: Did comes before the subject you; ask remains in its base form. Who is the object of ask.

common.sentence: What caused the loud noise outside last night?
common.meaning: asks which thing or event caused the noise

language_specific.usage: What is the subject of caused; no auxiliary is needed in this affirmative question.

common.sentence: What does this button do on the coffee maker?
common.meaning: marks a present-tense question about the button's function

language_specific.usage: Does precedes the third-person singular subject this button; the main verb do stays in its base form.

common.sentence: Which bus stops closest to the public library?
common.meaning: asks for the bus that makes the stop

language_specific.usage: Which bus is the subject of stops. Bus is a count noun: one bus, two buses; take a bus.

common.sentence: Which bus do we take to the public library?
common.meaning: marks a present-tense question about the bus to take

language_specific.usage: Do precedes the subject we; which bus is the object of take.

common.sentence: Who can open the store early on Saturday?
common.meaning: asks which person is able to open the store

language_specific.usage: Who is the subject of can open; the modal follows it.

common.sentence: Who can we call if the heat stops working?
common.meaning: asks about an available person to call

language_specific.usage: Can precedes the subject we; who is the object of call.

common.sentence: Who is waiting outside the dentist's office now?
common.meaning: asks which person is doing an action now

language_specific.usage: Who is the subject of the question. Is combines with waiting to form the present progressive; no do is needed.

common.sentence: Who are you waiting for outside the theater?
common.meaning: forms the present progressive question about the person being awaited

language_specific.usage: Are precedes the subject you. Who is the object of for, which naturally remains after waiting.

common.sentence: Which lights were flashing during the power outage?
common.meaning: forms the past progressive question about the lights

language_specific.usage: Were agrees with the plural subject which lights and combines with flashing.

common.sentence: Which room was the visitor looking for this morning?
common.meaning: forms the past progressive question about the room

language_specific.usage: Was precedes the third-person singular subject the visitor. Which room is the object of for.

common.sentence: Who didn't receive the schedule for next week?
common.meaning: forms a negative past-tense question about the person who did not receive the schedule
common.part_of_speech: contracted auxiliary verb and negative particle

language_specific.usage: Who is the subject. The negative auxiliary didn't is followed by the base form receive.

common.sentence: Who didn't you see at the neighborhood meeting?
common.meaning: forms a negative past-tense question about a person you did not see
common.part_of_speech: contracted auxiliary verb and negative particle

language_specific.usage: Didn't precedes the subject you; who is the object of see.

common.sentence: What keeps the screen from turning off so quickly?
common.meaning: prevents something from happening

language_specific.usage: Keep someone or something from doing something means prevent it. Here what is the subject, so the verb takes keeps.

common.sentence: What are the children making for the school fair?
common.meaning: forms the present progressive question about what is being made

language_specific.usage: Are precedes the plural subject the children; what is the object of making.

common.sentence: Which neighbor has a spare key to your apartment?
common.meaning: possesses a spare key

language_specific.usage: Has is the third-person singular present form of have. Which neighbor is the subject.

common.sentence: Which key does your neighbor have for the apartment?
common.meaning: marks a present-tense question about the key

language_specific.usage: Does precedes the third-person singular subject your neighbor; have stays in its base form.

common.sentence: Who has already signed up for the weekend trip?
common.meaning: forms a question about who has registered so far

language_specific.usage: Who is the subject; has combines with signed to form the present perfect.

common.sentence: Who have you chosen to lead the group?
common.meaning: forms a question about the person selected

language_specific.usage: Have precedes the subject you and combines with chosen. Who is the object of chosen.

common.sentence: What fell off the shelf during the storm?
common.meaning: dropped from a higher place

language_specific.usage: Fell is the past tense of fall; what is its subject.

common.sentence: What did the wind knock off the shelf?
common.meaning: marks a past-tense question about the thing the wind knocked down

language_specific.usage: Did precedes the subject the wind; knock stays in its base form. What is the object of knock.

common.sentence: Who lives across the hall from your cousin?
common.meaning: has a home in a place

language_specific.usage: Who is the subject, and lives is the third-person singular present form.

common.sentence: Who does your cousin live with in Chicago?
common.meaning: indicates the person who shares a home with your cousin

language_specific.usage: Live with someone means share a home with them. Who is the object of with, which naturally stays at the end of this question.

common.sentence: Which students need extra time on the assignment?
common.meaning: asks which students require extra time

language_specific.usage: Which students is the plural subject of need. Student is a count noun: one student, two students; a student needs time.

common.sentence: Which students should we notify about the room change?
common.meaning: asks which students it would be appropriate to notify

language_specific.usage: Should precedes the subject we; which students is the object of notify.

common.sentence: Who is responsible for locking the office tonight?
common.meaning: asks which person has the responsibility

language_specific.usage: Who is the subject of is; responsible describes that person.

common.sentence: Who did you lend your spare key to?
common.meaning: identifies the person receiving something

language_specific.usage: Lend something to someone means let that person borrow it. In Who did you lend something to?, who asks for the recipient and to stays at the end.

common.sentence: What would make this chair more comfortable for you?
common.meaning: asks about a possible change that could improve the chair

language_specific.usage: What is the subject of would make; the modal follows the subject.

common.sentence: What would you change about this chair for comfort?
common.meaning: asks about a change you might make

language_specific.usage: Would precedes the subject you; what is the object of change.

common.sentence: I don't know whether the pharmacy is open today.
common.meaning: lack the answer

language_specific.usage: Not know whether or if something is true expresses a lack of knowledge. The embedded question has statement order: the pharmacy is open.

common.sentence: I'm wondering if Maya received the updated schedule.
common.meaning: wanting to know

language_specific.usage: Wonder if or whether something happened means want to know the answer. The embedded question has statement order: Maya received.

common.sentence: Please check whether the back door is locked.
common.meaning: find out whether something is true

language_specific.usage: Check whether or if something is true means verify its status. The embedded question has statement order: the back door is locked.

common.sentence: Could you tell me if this train stops downtown?
common.meaning: give me the answer
common.part_of_speech: verb, object pronoun, and subordinating conjunction

language_specific.usage: Tell someone if or whether something is true means give that person the answer. The recipient follows tell; the embedded question has statement order: this train stops.

common.sentence: We need to find out whether the tickets are refundable.
common.meaning: discover the answer

language_specific.usage: Find out whether or if something is true means discover the answer. With a noun object, say find out the answer or find the answer out; a pronoun goes before out: find it out.

common.sentence: I'm not sure if we have enough plates for everyone.
common.meaning: uncertain

language_specific.usage: Be not sure if or whether something is true expresses uncertainty. The embedded question has statement order: we have enough plates.

common.sentence: Let me know whether or not you can attend.
common.meaning: introduces both possible answers about attending

language_specific.usage: Let someone know whether or not something is true asks for an answer either way. The embedded question uses statement order: you can attend.

common.sentence: Can you see if the oven has reached 350 degrees?
common.meaning: check whether something is true

language_specific.usage: See if or whether something is true can mean check it. Here if introduces an embedded question, not a condition; the clause has statement order.

common.sentence: I can't remember whether I turned off the stove.
common.meaning: cannot recall the answer

language_specific.usage: Not remember whether or if something happened expresses a lack of recall. The embedded question has statement order: I turned off the stove.

common.sentence: I don't know whether to leave now or wait.
common.meaning: introduces a choice about an action

language_specific.usage: Use whether to plus a base verb to introduce a choice of action, as in whether to leave now or wait. If cannot directly replace whether before a to-infinitive here.

common.sentence: The trip depends on whether the roads are safe.
common.meaning: is determined by

language_specific.usage: Use depend on a condition or depend on it to say that an outcome is affected by that condition. In depend on whether the roads are safe, on comes before the whether clause; depend on is not separable.

common.sentence: We talked about whether the store should stay open later.
common.meaning: introduces the question being discussed

language_specific.usage: Use talk about whether followed by a clause. After the preposition about, use whether rather than if.

common.sentence: She asked whether we wanted tea or coffee.
common.meaning: connects two alternatives in the question

language_specific.usage: Whether introduces the embedded question, and or connects the explicit alternatives tea and coffee.

common.sentence: I'm trying to decide whether to drive or take the bus.
common.meaning: choose between possible actions

language_specific.usage: Use decide whether to followed by a verb to describe a choice of action. A second option can follow or.

common.sentence: The landlord is here. Please ask her if pets are allowed.
common.meaning: request an answer from her about whether something is true
common.part_of_speech: verb phrase with pronoun object and conjunction

language_specific.usage: Use ask someone if or whether followed by a clause in statement order. The recipient comes between ask and if; her refers to the landlord.

common.sentence: I doubt whether this old printer will work today.
common.meaning: think something may not be true

language_specific.usage: Use doubt whether followed by a clause in statement order to express uncertainty about a possible result.

common.sentence: The coach questioned whether the field was dry enough.
common.meaning: expressed doubt about

language_specific.usage: Use question whether followed by a clause to express doubt about something.

common.sentence: Does it matter whether we arrive before noon?
common.meaning: be important

language_specific.usage: Use it matters whether followed by a clause to say that the answer affects the situation. The embedded clause keeps statement order.

common.sentence: I'm curious whether the new cafe serves breakfast.
common.meaning: interested in finding out

language_specific.usage: Use be curious whether or be curious if followed by a clause in statement order.

common.sentence: Can you confirm whether the meeting starts at nine?
common.meaning: establish or state the answer

language_specific.usage: Use confirm whether or confirm if followed by a clause to ask for verification.

common.sentence: It's unclear whether the museum will open on Monday.
common.meaning: not known whether something is true

language_specific.usage: Use it is unclear whether followed by a clause in statement order to describe an unanswered question.

common.sentence: I wonder whether Sam hasn't received my message yet.
common.meaning: forms the negative present perfect in an embedded question
common.part_of_speech: contracted auxiliary verb and negative particle

language_specific.usage: Hasn't is has not. Sam is third-person singular, so the embedded clause uses has before the past participle received.

common.sentence: We need to establish whether anyone can unlock the gate.
common.meaning: is able to

language_specific.usage: In an embedded question, can follows the subject and precedes the base verb: whether anyone can unlock.

common.sentence: I'm unsure whether we should book a table or wait.
common.meaning: expresses a possible advisable action

language_specific.usage: In the embedded question, should follows the subject we and precedes the base verb book.

common.sentence: The new ramp makes it easier to move boxes inside.

common.sentence: The meeting ran over, so I missed the earlier train.

common.sentence: After several failed attempts to fix the lamp, I persisted.

common.meaning: unhappy because something was not as good as one had hoped

language_specific.usage: Postpone an event until a later time, or postpone doing something.
